title: -ing clauses (He hurt his knee playing football.)
subtitle: playing football / having finished
summary: Use an -ing clause to say that two things happen at the same time, and Having (done) or Not -ing to give the reason or the earlier action.

lesson.heading: Two things at the same time
lesson.text: Kate is in the kitchen. She's making coffee. You can put the two ideas together: **Kate is in the kitchen making coffee.** Use an **-ing clause** like this when two things happen at the same time.

examples.text: A man ran out of the house **shouting**.
examples.note: = he ran out of the house and he was shouting

examples.text: Do something! Don't just stand there **doing** nothing!

lesson.heading: One action during another
lesson.text: We also use **-ing** when one action happens during another, longer action. You can also say **while doing** something or **when doing** something.

examples.text: Joe hurt his knee **while playing** football.

lesson.heading: Having (done) - the earlier action
lesson.text: When one action happens *before* something else, we use **having (done)** for the first action. You can also say **after -ing**. These structures are used more in written English than in spoken English.

examples.text: **Having found** a hotel, we looked for somewhere to eat.
**Having finished** her work, she went home.
**After finishing** her work, she went home.

lesson.note: When a sentence begins with Having (done something) or After (doing something), we write a comma after that part of the sentence.

lesson.heading: -ing to say why
lesson.text: You can also use **-ing** to explain something, or to say why somebody does something. The sentence usually begins with the -ing clause. For a negative, begin with **Not -ing**.

examples.text: **Feeling** tired, I went to bed early.
**Being** unemployed, he doesn't have much money.
**Not having** a car, she finds it difficult to get around.
examples.note: = because she doesn't have a car

examples.text: **Not knowing** what to do, I called my friend to ask her advice.

lesson.heading: Having (done) to say why
lesson.text: We use **having (done)** when the reason is something that was complete before the other thing happened.

examples.text: **Having seen** the film twice, I didn't want to see it again.
examples.note: = because I had seen it twice

examples.text: **Having spent** nearly all our money, we couldn't afford to stay at a hotel.

lesson.text: Don't forget the comma: when the sentence starts with the -ing clause (*Feeling tired, ...* / *Having seen ..., ...*), a comma closes that part of the sentence.

exercises.prompt: Match each situation with the -ing clause that completes it.

pairs.left: Amy was sitting in an armchair

pairs.right: trying not to make a noise.
saying she would be back in an hour.

pairs.left: Lisa worked in Rome for two years,

pairs.right: looking at the sights and taking pictures.

exercises.prompt: Lisa worked in Rome for two years, ___ English.
exercises.explanation: The two things happened at the same time, so we use an -ing clause.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.
exercises.answer: I got very wet walking in the rain.
exercises.explanation: Getting wet happened during the walk, so the -ing clause comes at the end.

exercises.prompt: My friend slipped and fell ___ off a bus.
exercises.explanation: One action happened during the other: he fell while he was getting off.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.
exercises.answer: Laura had an accident driving to work.
exercises.explanation: = while she was driving to work.

exercises.prompt: I didn't have a phone, so I had no way of contacting anyone. Rewrite this with an -ing clause.
options: Not having a phone, I had no way of contacting anyone.
Having not a phone, I had no way of contacting anyone.
Not to have a phone, I had no way of contacting anyone.
exercises.explanation: The negative of an -ing clause is Not + -ing.

exercises.prompt: I thought they might be hungry, so I offered them something to eat. -> ___ they might be hungry, I offered them something to eat.
exercises.explanation: An -ing clause at the start of a sentence gives the reason: Thinking they might be hungry, ...

exercises.prompt: Robert is a vegetarian, so he doesn't eat any kind of meat. -> ___ a vegetarian, Robert doesn't eat any kind of meat.
exercises.explanation: Being a vegetarian = because he is a vegetarian.

exercises.prompt: ___ our tickets, we went into the theatre and took our seats.
exercises.explanation: Buying the tickets was complete before we went in, so we use Having + past participle.

exercises.prompt: ___ his job recently, James is now unemployed.
exercises.explanation: The reason happened earlier and is complete: Having lost his job, ...

exercises.statement: Being seen the film twice, I didn't want to see it again.
exercises.explanation: Having seen the film twice, I didn't want to see it again. For an action that was complete earlier we use Having + past participle.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.
exercises.answer: Two people were overcome by smoke trying to put out the fire.
exercises.explanation: = while they were trying to put out the fire.
